note.explanation: In dynamic equilibrium, a reversible reaction continues in both directions. The forward and backward reactions happen at equal rates, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant.
examples: In a sealed flask, colourless N₂O₄ changes into brown NO₂. As NO₂ forms, the reverse reaction also starts; at equilibrium, the brown colour stops changing.
In a closed container of water at a fixed temperature, evaporation and condensation can occur at equal rates.
note.checkAnswer: At dynamic equilibrium, forward and backward reaction rates are equal, and the concentrations remain constant.
note.simple: The reaction has not stopped. Both directions keep happening, but they balance each other, so the amounts of reactants and products do not change.
note.checkQuestion: What happens to the concentrations of reactants and products at dynamic equilibrium?
note.title: Dynamic Equilibrium
steps: A reversible reaction starts in the forward direction.
Products build up and begin to react in the backward direction.
The forward and backward reaction rates become equal.
The reaction continues in both directions, while concentrations stay constant.
note.answer: The reaction continues in both directions at equal rates, so the concentrations of reacting species remain constant.

options: Both reactions stop completely.
The forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates.
All reactants have changed into products.
The backward reaction becomes faster than the forward reaction.
mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes a reversible reaction at dynamic equilibrium?
rationales: This is wrong because the reaction continues rather than stopping.
This is right because equal rates keep the concentrations constant while both reactions continue.
This is wrong because equilibrium does not require all reactants to be used up.
This is wrong because at equilibrium the backward rate is equal to, not greater than, the forward rate.

options: They keep increasing.

rationales: This is wrong because the forward reaction is balanced by the backward reaction.
This is wrong because the backward reaction is balanced by the forward reaction.
This is right because equal reaction rates mean there is no overall change in concentration.
This is wrong because equilibrium does not mean that all reacting species disappear.

options: Only the forward reaction continues.
Only the backward reaction continues.
Both reactions continue.

mcqs.stem: Why is chemical equilibrium called dynamic?
rationales: This is wrong because the backward reaction also continues at equilibrium.
This is wrong because the forward reaction also continues at equilibrium.
This is right because both directions keep occurring even though concentrations stay constant.

options: The forward reaction begins to slow down.

rationales: This is not the key event described; the important change is that the backward reaction begins.
This is right because accumulated products react to form reactants in the reverse reaction.
This is wrong because the reaction remains reversible.
This is wrong because products react backward but do not disappear immediately.

rationales: This is right because both the reaction's nature and the conditions affect the time.
This is wrong because equilibrium is not reached instantly in every reaction.
This is wrong because some reactions reach equilibrium within seconds or minutes.

rationales: This is wrong because brown NO₂ forms from colourless N₂O₄.

rationales: This is wrong because the forward reaction continues.

rationales: This is wrong because the section's sealed-flask example can approach equilibrium.

written.text: How is dynamic equilibrium different from the static equilibrium?
written.finalAnswer: In dynamic equilibrium, the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates and concentrations remain constant. In static equilibrium, no change or movement is taking place.

rubric.why: This states what makes dynamic equilibrium dynamic.
rubric.description: States that both reactions continue at equal rates.
rubric.how: Mention the continuing forward and backward reactions and that their rates are equal.

rubric.why: This clearly contrasts dynamic equilibrium with a static state.
rubric.description: States that static equilibrium has no change or movement.
rubric.how: Explain that a static state has no continuing reaction or movement.

modelAnswer: In dynamic equilibrium, the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates.
In static equilibrium, no change or movement is taking place.

written.text: How can you decrease the time to attain the position of equilibrium in a reversible reaction?
written.finalAnswer: Use a catalyst and suitable conditions to increase the reaction rates; for example, the ammonia reaction reaches equilibrium within minutes at around 400°C in the presence of a catalyst.

rubric.why: A catalyst can make the reaction reach equilibrium sooner.
rubric.description: Names a catalyst as a way to decrease the time.
rubric.how: State that a catalyst should be used.

rubric.why: The reaction reaches equilibrium sooner when its reactions are reasonably fast.
rubric.description: Links faster reaction rates or the textbook ammonia example to shorter time.
rubric.how: Explain that rates become faster, or give the ammonia example at around 400°C with a catalyst.

modelAnswer: Use a catalyst and suitable conditions to make the reaction rates faster.
For example, the formation and decomposition of ammonia are reasonably fast at around 400°C in the presence of a catalyst, so equilibrium is reached within minutes.

written.text: Do the phase changes in water (solid to liquid, liquid to vapour) reversible or irreversible?
written.finalAnswer: The phase changes in water are reversible: ice melts to liquid water and liquid water freezes to ice; liquid water evaporates to vapour and vapour condenses to liquid water.

rubric.why: This identifies the nature of the water phase changes.
rubric.description: States that the phase changes are reversible.
rubric.how: Answer that the changes are reversible.

rubric.why: Examples show that the changes can occur in both directions.
rubric.description: Gives at least one matching pair of opposite phase changes.
rubric.how: Give melting and freezing, or evaporation and condensation.

modelAnswer: The phase changes in water are reversible.
Ice melts to liquid water and liquid water freezes to ice.
Liquid water evaporates to vapour and vapour condenses to liquid water.

written.text: Explain how the rates of forward and backward reactions change when the system approaches equilibrium.
written.finalAnswer: At first, the forward reaction is faster and the backward reaction is slow because little product is present. As products build up, the backward reaction becomes faster. At equilibrium, the forward and backward rates are equal.

rubric.why: The forward reaction starts when the reactants are mixed.
rubric.description: States that the forward reaction is initially faster.
rubric.how: Describe the forward reaction as faster at the start.

rubric.why: The reverse reaction needs products to form first.
rubric.description: Explains that the backward reaction is initially slow because little product is present.
rubric.how: Link the small starting amount of product with a slow backward reaction.

rubric.why: More product allows the reverse reaction to proceed faster.
rubric.description: Describes the backward rate increasing as products build up.
rubric.how: Connect product formation with an increase in the backward reaction rate.

rubric.why: Equal forward and backward rates mark the equilibrium state.
rubric.description: Gives the rate relationship at equilibrium.
rubric.how: State that the two rates become equal.

modelAnswer: At first, the forward reaction is faster and the backward reaction is slow because little product is present.
As products build up, they react to form reactants, so the backward reaction becomes faster.
At equilibrium, the rate of the forward reaction becomes equal to the rate of the backward reaction.

written.text: Describe the effect of a catalyst on the reversible reaction.
written.finalAnswer: A catalyst makes the forward and backward reactions faster, so the system reaches equilibrium in less time. It does not stop either reaction.

rubric.why: The forward reaction is one of the two reactions affected.
rubric.description: States that a catalyst makes the forward reaction faster.
rubric.how: Mention the effect on the forward reaction.

rubric.why: The backward reaction must also be considered in a reversible system.
rubric.description: States that a catalyst makes the backward reaction faster.
rubric.how: Mention the effect on the backward reaction.

rubric.why: Faster reactions reduce the time needed to reach equilibrium.
rubric.description: Links the faster reactions to reaching equilibrium sooner.
rubric.how: State that equilibrium is reached in less time.

rubric.why: Equilibrium remains dynamic; reactions do not cease.
rubric.description: Makes clear that the reactions continue.
rubric.how: State that the catalyst does not stop the reactions.

modelAnswer: A catalyst makes the forward and backward reactions faster.
The system therefore reaches equilibrium in less time.
The reactions continue; they do not stop at equilibrium.

examTips: A short-answer question may ask for the meaning of dynamic equilibrium or how it differs from static equilibrium.
For a definition, include both key points: the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates, and concentrations remain constant.
A descriptive question may ask how the rates change as equilibrium is approached: the backward reaction begins as products build up, and the rates become equal at equilibrium.
If asked how quickly equilibrium is reached, explain that the time depends on the reaction and its conditions; use the textbook ammonia example if useful.

hints: Think of water changing from liquid to gas and back again.
Name the changes between all three states, and explain that equal opposing rates mean no overall change.
yourTurn.question: Elaborate an example of dynamic equilibrium which exists in this world between the three physical states of water.
solution: Water can exist as ice, liquid water and water vapour.
Ice melts to liquid water, while liquid water can freeze to ice.
Liquid water evaporates to vapour, while vapour can condense to liquid water.
In a suitable closed system at fixed conditions, opposing changes can occur at equal rates; the amounts in each state then remain constant overall.
yourTurn.answer: Water changes reversibly between ice, liquid water and water vapour. When opposing changes occur at equal rates, the amounts of the states remain constant overall.

yourTurn.question: Dinitrogen tetraoxide (N₂O₄) is a colourless gas. It slowly changes to brown coloured nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) at 100° C. Predict how the colour of the mixture will change if N₂O₄ is kept in a sealed flask at 100°C.
solution: At first, colourless N₂O₄ changes into brown NO₂, so the mixture becomes brown.
As NO₂ builds up, the reverse reaction also begins.
When the forward and backward reaction rates become equal, the concentrations stop changing.
The brown colour then remains at a constant shade.
yourTurn.answer: The mixture becomes brown as NO₂ forms. At equilibrium, its brown colour stops changing.

explain.title: A reversible reaction goes in two directions
explain.body: When a reversible reaction starts, it initially moves in the forward direction. As products build up, they can react to form the original reactants in the backward direction.

explain.title: The rates become equal
explain.body: At equilibrium, the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction. The reaction has not stopped; both directions continue.

explain.title: Concentrations stay constant
explain.body: Because the two directions balance, the concentrations of reacting species do not change overall at equilibrium. They do not have to be equal to each other.

explain.title: The time depends on the reaction
explain.body: The time taken to reach equilibrium depends on the nature of the reaction and the conditions. Your textbook gives the ammonia reaction at around 400°C with a catalyst as an example that reaches equilibrium within minutes.

mistakes: Do not write that the reaction stops at equilibrium; both directions continue.
Do not say that reactant and product concentrations must be equal; they remain constant, but need not be equal.
Do not confuse equal reaction rates with equal amounts of reactants and products.
When explaining the changing rates, remember that the backward reaction begins after products have built up.
